items.titel: Afghan pushback survivor fights ‘impossible’ evidence rules in European courts with new UN case against Greece
items.anriss: The survivor of a brutal pushback in Greece was forced to take action at UN level, in a display of the impossibly high standard of evidence required in European courts to prevent victims of pushbacks from accessing justice.

absaetze.t: The survivor of a brutal pushback in Greece was forced to take action at UN level, in a display of the impossibly high standard of evidence required in European courts to prevent victims of pushbacks from accessing justice.
A Hazara teenager’s flight from Afghanistan in 2018 during an uptick in Taliban violence against the minority, ended in a rubber dinghy ride from Turkey to Samos, a Greek island.

The 13 year-old had unsuccessfully attempted to obtain international protection in Iran, Turkey, and later in a refugee camp in Samos upon arriving in 2020, now aged 15. His requests to initiate an asylum procedure were ignored, and he was promptly hoisted onto a coast guard boat to Turkey.
The boy was handcuffed to another young traveller, and both had their phones and money stolen by Greek coast guards.

Despite providing photos, videos, locations shared in real time, Turkish Coast Guard and Frontex database records, the European Court of human rights (ECHR) rejected the case for lack of evidence in 2025.

Now granted refugee status in Europe, the young man tried overcoming the maze of obstacles which have so far prevented anyone from successfully pursued legal action against a pushback on Friday (30 October), submitting a claim to the UN’s Human Rights Committee against Greece.
The case represents an extraordinary mishandling of basic human rights, since pushback cases usually fail to see justice because there is usually no evidence of their arrival on European soil.
Yet here, the Afghan boy had made it all the way to the camp where they met asylum seekers that were known to them.

items.titel: Le discours de la victoire de Jon Ossoff
items.anriss: Le soir du 3 novembre 2026, à Atlanta, le démocrate Jon Ossoff a célébré sa réélection au Sénat des États-Unis pour la Géorgie, avec près de dix-huit points d’avance sur le républicain Mike Collins, soutenu par Donald Trump. Le même soir, …

absaetze.t: Le soir du 3 novembre 2026, à Atlanta, le démocrate Jon Ossoff a célébré sa réélection au Sénat des États-Unis pour la Géorgie, avec près de dix-huit points d’avance sur le républicain Mike Collins, soutenu par Donald Trump. Le même soir, la démocrate Keisha Lance Bottoms a remporté le poste de gouverneure de l’État.

Avant même d’évoquer sa réélection en Géorgie, Ossoff a salué la victoire du « peuple américain » sur Trump et la « survie de notre république », puis a dressé un diagnostic de la vie quotidienne des Américains et a esquissé une vision du monde. En invoquant « ce grand esprit national qui a vaincu le fascisme, créé la Sécurité sociale, envoyé des hommes sur la Lune et fait adopter les lois sur les droits civiques », il s’est implicitement placé dans la lignée de Roosevelt, Kennedy et Johnson, se posant ainsi en présidentiable.

Bonsoir, Atlanta ! Merci, Géorgie. Géorgie, vous avez réussi ! Et permettez-moi d’être le premier à adresser publiquement mes félicitations à la gouverneure élue de l’État de Géorgie, Keisha Lance Bottoms.

À chaque bénévole qui s’est donné corps et âme à cette campagne, et à tous ceux qui ont mis la main au portefeuille pour que nous puissions tenir tête aux super PAC financés par l’argent occulte : merci.
À Charlie Bailey et à son équipe, qui ont fait du Parti démocrate de Géorgie le plus puissant qu’il ait été depuis une génération : merci.
À mon équipe, à Ellen, Keenan, Rey, Miryam, Chandra et à la meilleure équipe de la politique américaine : merci.
À ma merveilleuse épouse Alisha et à mes filles Eva et Lila, à mes parents et à toute ma famille : merci pour votre amour et votre soutien inconditionnels.
Et aux habitants du grand État de Géorgie, pour la confiance que vous m’avez accordée en me permettant de continuer à vous représenter au Sénat des États-Unis : merci, merci, merci.
Maintenant, Géorgie.
Merci.
[LA FOULE : « JE T’AIME »]
Moi aussi, je vous aime. Moi aussi, je vous aime.
Écoutez !

Par des victoires larges et décisives, le peuple américain a répudié la dépravation, la corruption et l’incompétence du président Donald J. Trump, « canard boiteux ». Et si, par moments au cours de ces deux dernières années, sous l’assaut incessant de la brutalité et de l’indécence, vous avez douté de la survie de notre république, que les résultats de ce soir vous redonnent courage : les premières lueurs de l’aube pointent à l’horizon.

Mais souvenez-vous que, dans les salons, dans les jardins et lors des meetings à travers la Géorgie ces deux dernières années, nous avons affirmé ensemble que notre tâche n’est pas seulement de contenir la malfaisance d’un président, mais de guérir la fracture plus profonde qui la sous-tend.

Que ce moment est une ouverture, non pour une restauration, mais pour une réforme profonde. Et donc, au milieu de notre célébration de ce soir, nous devons reconnaître que la crise de fond qui étreint notre république demeure, et que, par conséquent, notre travail le plus essentiel reste à faire.

Car tandis que les riches et les bien représentés par les lobbies se gavent d’informations privilégiées et de faveurs officielles, les familles oubliées de l’Amérique sont traitées avec un mépris systématique de la part des entreprises et une indifférence officielle ; elles travaillent de plus en plus dur tandis que le tapis de course s’accélère et s’incline toujours davantage, et que les factures sont toujours plus élevées.

Au lieu de lire à votre fille son livre préféré pendant cette précieuse heure de liberté après le travail, vous êtes au téléphone à supplier votre assureur de prendre en charge le médicament qui empêche ses crises d’épilepsie. Vous signalez les moisissures noires à votre propriétaire, qui ne répare pas la fuite, et l’ambulance appelée pour la crise d’asthme de votre tout-petit est suivie d’une facture de 3 000 dollars.

Pour trop de gens, devenir propriétaire relève du rêve inaccessible. Les exploitations familiales sont au bord de la ruine, et alors que les soins de santé n’ont jamais coûté aussi cher, les plastiques envahissent nos corps, notre sang et le lait maternel. Des « polluants éternels » toxiques contaminent l’eau potable de la moitié du pays, et les pollueurs ont reçu un nouveau permis pour empoisonner notre air.

À l’étranger, la crédibilité et le leadership américains sont en déclin, et le monde se réarme en vue d’un conflit mondial. Et, à nos risques et périls, l’humanité oublie à toute vitesse les terribles leçons des deux guerres mondiales et de la Shoah.

Pendant ce temps, les titans de la Silicon Valley se creusent des bunkers et préviennent que l’intelligence artificielle qu’ils créent fait courir à l’humanité un risque d’extinction. Et face à ces défis d’une portée et d’une complexité sans précédent, même si nous célébrons à juste titre la victoire historique de ce soir, le fait est que nous sommes depuis trop longtemps enlisés dans une politique mesquine et égoïste, achetée par les grandes fortunes, détachée de tout principe moral solide et résignée à des divisions insurmontables.
Autrement dit, les États-Unis dérivent dans la tempête. Mais, Géorgie, nous pouvons reprendre en main notre destin, et nous le ferons.

Ce soir, nous avons porté un coup nécessaire et décisif en faveur de la justice et du progrès. Et ce soir, en Géorgie, nous avons prouvé non seulement que l’unité est possible, mais que nous pouvons surmonter la division sans rien céder sur nos objectifs.

Dans chaque recoin de la Géorgie, cette campagne a plaidé pour la nécessité d’interdire l’argent des entreprises et l’argent occulte en politique, pour un leadership américain au service de la paix et des droits humains dans le monde, et pour la garantie de soins de santé pour chaque Américain, sans exception.

Nous nous sommes engagés à poursuivre le travail visant à mettre au pas Big Pharma, les grands assureurs et les géants de la tech pour défendre les familles géorgiennes en difficulté ; et sur cette base, nous avons bâti une nouvelle majorité qui s’étend bien au-delà des clivages partisans. Le fondement de cette nouvelle majorité, c’est la confiance : une confiance bâtie au fil d’années d’appels téléphoniques aux maires, aux pasteurs et aux agriculteurs, une confiance qui se mesure aux problèmes résolus ensemble, sans considération d’idéologie ou d’appartenance partisane.

Je remercie les maires républicains Matheson, Smith et Fry, de Valdosta, Tifton et Toccoa, ainsi que les innombrables autres responsables républicains qui ont rejoint notre équipe. Et je remercie les centaines de milliers d’électeurs indépendants et républicains qui ont rejoint notre coalition victorieuse. Ne doutez jamais que l’unité soit possible.

Même dans ses derniers mois, le représentant John Lewis nous rappelait toujours que nous vivons tous dans une seule maison : la maison américaine. Vous vous en souvenez ? Dans une seule maison du monde. Il appelait cela la vérité inéluctable selon laquelle nous sommes tous membres d’une même famille humaine.

Et je sais que beaucoup d’entre vous se sont donnés corps et âme à cette campagne, non pas pour moi ni pour le Parti démocrate, mais parce que vous êtes profondément bouleversés par la souffrance que nos semblables endurent en ce moment : la terreur d’une enfant qui regarde l’ICE emmener sa mère, le désespoir d’un patient atteint d’un cancer qui perd sa couverture en plein traitement. Mais cette douleur dans votre cœur, cette boule au ventre, ce sentiment, c’est ce qui nous rappelle que nous sommes tous dans le même bateau, que nous ne sommes pas seulement les États-Unis, mais un peuple uni. E pluribus unum. De plusieurs, un seul. Et au fil des siècles, malgré nos péchés et grâce à des luttes courageuses, la flamme de la liberté américaine a brillé d’un éclat toujours plus vif et plus audacieux, et a donné de l’espoir au monde entier.

Nous avons trébuché. Nous avons failli nous égarer. Mais, Géorgie, malgré toutes nos difficultés, je vous l’assure ce soir : portés par cette victoire historique et indéniable, nous les surmonterons, je ne doute pas un instant. Et notre tâche est désormais de réveiller ce grand esprit national qui a vaincu le fascisme et créé la Social Security, qui a envoyé des hommes sur la Lune et fait adopter les lois sur les droits civiques, afin de relever les défis et d’assumer les obligations de notre temps. Car je refuse que mes deux petites filles grandissent dans un monde aussi sombre, dangereux et cruel que celui-ci menace de le devenir.

Je refuse qu’Eva et Lila grandissent avec des IA pour amis et pour professeurs, dans une société où les malades meurent non pas parce qu’il n’existe pas de remède, mais parce qu’ils n’ont pas d’argent. Où nous avons assez d’armes nucléaires pour détruire le monde mille fois, mais où nous refusons de garantir des soins de santé à chaque citoyen. Sur une planète empoisonnée, qui se réarme pour une guerre mondiale, où la vie humaine ne vaut rien et où la force prime le droit.

Voyez-vous, quand Eva sera assez grande pour me demander pourquoi j’ai laissé faire cela, je veux pouvoir lui répondre en toute vérité que je ne l’ai pas laissé faire. Je lui raconterai comment, l’année même de ses cinq ans, la Géorgie a surmonté tous les doutes et tous les coups bas, non seulement pour gagner, mais pour tracer une nouvelle voie pour notre État, notre pays et notre monde.

Que nous avons défendu le droit de vote et les droits civiques chez nous. Que nous avons rétabli le leadership américain en faveur de la paix et des droits humains dans le monde. Que nous avons enfin agi pour interdire l’argent des entreprises et l’argent occulte dans notre vie politique, et que nous avons garanti des soins de santé à chaque Américain, sans exception.
Merci, Géorgie. Ce soir, nous célébrons cette victoire, et demain, nous nous remettons au travail. Merci beaucoup. Merci, Géorgie. Merci. Merci.

items.titel: Democratic Socialists of America see record wins in US midterm elections
items.anriss: The left-wing movement has won support for its views on issues like the war in Gaza and universal healthcare.

absaetze.t: The left-wing movement has won support for its views on issues like the war in Gaza and universal healthcare.

A record number of candidates for federal offices who were backed by or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) won in Tuesday’s US midterm elections, marking the most successful night the left-leaning movement has had in national politics so far.

“This is a record for the DSA; these are numbers we have not seen in over a hundred years in socialist electoral activity,” National Electoral Commission member Chanpreet Singh said on a livestream on Tuesday night after the elections. The stream, broadcast on Twitch to more than 200,000 viewers, was hosted by political commentator Hasan Piker.

The political group saw a surge in membership in 2016, when Vermont’s US Senator Bernie Sanders, a prominent DSA member, ran unsuccessfully for president, bringing the movement’s views on issues like universal healthcare and housing to a broader audience. The election of Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York City in 2025 brought more attention, and more members, to the DSA.

Today the movement says it has more than 120,000 members, with chapters across all 50 states. Members vote to decide which candidates to back in elections, in federal contests like those for the US Congress, as well as state and local bodies. Many of the candidates that the DSA endorses share views on core issues, including the war in Gaza, healthcare, and immigration.
So where did DSA-affiliated candidates win federal offices on November 3?

In New York State, three candidates who were either officially endorsed by the chapter or were closely affiliated with the DSA were elected to office on Tuesday: Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier, and Brad Lander were elected to the US House of Representatives for the first time, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was re-elected to her seat. Chevalier, who worked on Mamdani’s mayoral campaign, has helped organise pro-Palestinian protests and has been vocal about her opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza.

In Michigan, DSA member Rashida Tlaib was re-elected to her seat in the US House, member Donavan McKinney was elected to the body for the first time, and William Lawrence defeated a Republican candidate for a highly competitive US House seat.

Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old immigrant from Ethiopia who has also been outspoken on her views on issues like opposing Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was elected to office with a wide margin to represent Colorado in the House.
In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, voters elected Chris Rabb, a former state lawmaker, to the US House for the first time.
On the West Coast in Los Angeles, California, Angela Gonzales-Torres defeated a Democratic incumbent for a seat in the US House.

Adam Hamawy, a former US Army medical doctor who has worked as a surgeon in Gaza, won a district in New Jersey. Although he is not a DSA member, he has aligned himself with the movement and campaigned alongside DSA-backed candidates.

items.titel: Sudan factories struggle to restart after devastating wartime losses
items.anriss: War has left Sudanese workers jobless and consumers facing higher prices as factories struggle to reopen.

absaetze.t: Khartoum, Sudan – Mansour Gaily’s factory in Khartoum produced sweets for local consumers and provided employment for workers.

But when fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, production ground to a halt, like thousands of other businesses across the country.
More than three years later, Gaily faces the challenge of bringing his business back to life. Production may have resumed, but the factory is only operating at 40 percent of its previous capacity.
“Our losses are estimated at $1m,” Gaily told Al Jazeera. “We lost some machinery, spare parts, and needed to rebuild large parts of the factory.”

Gaily’s troubles are typical of Sudan’s devastated manufacturing sector. Before the war, Khartoum was one of the country’s main industrial centres, home to factories producing food, textiles and other consumer goods.

However, Khartoum became a major battleground between the SAF and the RSF during the war, and although there have only been sporadic attacks since the army fully recaptured it last year, the industrial sector has not been rebuilt.
According to Sudan’s Ministry of Industry, approximately 1,800 industrial facilities have been damaged during the war, including 650 factories that were completely destroyed.
The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing a sector that is essential to employment, domestic production and economic recovery.
Abdulelah Mohamed owns a factory for plastic products and recycling in Khartoum. He describes the situation as catastrophic.
“Damaging, destroying and looting the factories was systematic. We lost everything,” Mohamed said. “The industrial sector needs new planning and a new vision so Sudan can produce things again.”
Economic needs

The damage extends beyond buildings and machinery. Raw materials, finished goods and equipment have been destroyed or looted, while electricity shortages, damaged transport networks and rising import costs have made reopening difficult even for businesses whose premises survived the fighting.

Sara Elfatih Khalil, chief executive of Al Teital Advance Industries, is among the manufacturers confronting these challenges. Her company’s factory in Khartoum produced sesame oil and, before the war, provided employment for 300 workers. Its warehouses have been looted during the fighting, and with damaged buildings and a supply chain that remains broken, the factory continues to be shut down.
“I believe industry will remain a cornerstone of any economic recovery and that it is capable of recovering rapidly if the basic conditions are met,” Khalil said.

“Restoring our confidence as investors requires security and political stability, clear and consistent economic policies, legal protection for investment and property rights, and reliable financing and infrastructure,” Khalil said. “Our situation is not unique. Less than 10 percent of factories in the sector are currently operational, and those that remain open are operating intermittently, with costs that threaten their continued viability.”

For Gaily, restoring production at his sweets factory requires a steady supply of ingredients, including sesame and sugar, as well as packaging, spare parts, electricity and workers. Disruption to any of these can bring production to a halt.

“We are operating at 40 percent of our production capacity because the damage was severe and capital is limited,” he said. “Despite the lost spare parts and the lack of labourers, we chose to continue because we don’t have any other options.”

Other manufacturers face similar obstacles. Some now must import materials that were previously available locally, increasing costs and making production vulnerable to further disruptions in transport and supply.

The problems also extend to financing. Businesses that have lost machinery, stock and income during the war often lack the capital needed to replace equipment and pay for stock and employees before sales resume.
Impact on workers and consumers
The consequences have extended to workers who depend on factories for their livelihoods.
Mohamed Haj is a worker who lost his job at a different sweets factory in Khartoum North and has struggled to find alternative employment.

“I lost my job at the beginning of the war, and the factory owner is unable to restore it,” Haj said. “Reviving the industrial sector in general could provide jobs for thousands of workers who have been left without work.”
At the other end of the supply chain, shopkeepers are struggling with the reduced availability of locally manufactured goods.
Abdelgadir Mohamed, who sells sweets and other consumer products in Bahri Central Market, said the disappearance of many Sudanese-made products has made it harder for traders to source stock.
“In some cases the imported products are cheaper for us and for the consumers,” the shopkeeper said, “but many of my customers prefer the Sudanese-made ones.”

Imports have partly filled the gap, but for shopkeepers this can mean higher purchasing costs and uncertain supplies, and for consumers already facing a decline in purchasing power, that adds pressure on household budgets.

“The prices are changing every day,” said Ahmed Mahmoud, a local consumer. “The local products’ prices are high and imported ones are also high, but for sweets like tahniya [a local sesame-based sweet], I prefer the Sudanese-made one.”

Sudanese authorities are now seeking to fix some of the damage. In August, a Ministry of Industry committee was established to assess the condition of industrial facilities in Khartoum State and prepare incentives to encourage factory owners to reopen. The recovery plan also includes restoring essential services in industrial areas, including electricity, water, roads, sewage and waste management.
The services are critical for manufacturers hoping to resume operations, but factory owners say reconstruction would require more than just restoring infrastructure.
Many factory owners need capital, and representatives of the Sudanese Chamber of Commerce say businesses need real, practical assistance, rather than just promises from authorities.
Rebuilding, or starting again?
Economist Mohamed Elnayer believes reconstruction offers an opportunity to address longstanding weaknesses in Sudan’s industrial economy.
“Rebuilding the industrial sector will require a broader strategy that addresses the structural weaknesses that existed even before the war,” Elnayer said.

Before the war, Khartoum was the industrial heart of Sudan, with the country’s factories largely concentrated inside it. That caused an inequality in opportunities between Khartoum and the rest of the country before the war, but a different problem arose during the conflict, when the capital became a major front line.

Many factories were destroyed and looted as a result, and analysts like Elnayer believe that the industrial sector should be rebuilt across Sudan. This would serve the dual purpose of avoiding any future paralysis of the industrial sector if fighting were to break out in the capital again, and also spread economic benefits around the country.

“Sudan needs to consider, before reconstruction, whether to simply restore the industrial sector that existed before the conflict, or provide an opportunity to develop a more competitive and productive economy in other Sudanese states,” he added.
For Gaily, those broader economy questions are inseparable from the practical challenge of keeping his factory running.
He hopes to repair the machinery, secure the ingredients needed to manufacture sweets and bring his former employees back.

“We need stronger support from the authorities by facilitating production, rehabilitating infrastructure and adopting stronger policies to encourage factory owners,” Gaily said. “Above all, the industrial sector needs financial support and coordinated efforts by stakeholders to sustain economic recovery.”

items.titel: Spain: Madrid hosts 30th Ibero-American Summit with 22-nation bloc
items.anriss: Spain is hosting the 30th Ibero-American Summit in Madrid, bringing together leaders from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking nations. The gathering aims to strengthen cooperation across Europe and Latin America.

absaetze.t: Spain is hosting the 30th Ibero-American Summit in Madrid, bringing together leaders from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking nations. The gathering aims to strengthen cooperation across Europe and Latin America.

World leaders gathered at Madrid's Teatro Real on Wednesday evening as King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia inaugurated the 30th Ibero-American Summit. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez greeted arriving delegations from the 22-member community.
ADVERTISEMENT

Despite the ceremonial welcome, only 10 countries were represented by their heads of state or government. Argentina's Javier Milei, Chile's José Antonio Kast and Guatemala's Bernardo Arévalo were among the seven Latin American presidents present.

Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum and Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodríguez stayed away, highlighting political divisions ahead of Spain's general election on 29 November.
UN chief António Guterres and European Council President António Costa joined the gathering, while Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky travelled to Madrid for separate talks.
Thursday's programme includes the plenary session and official photograph at the Royal Collections Gallery, as Spain mourns 69 victims of last week's train disaster.

items.titel: Zelenski makes surprise visit to Madrid for talks with Sánchez and Latin American leaders
items.anriss: Zelensky visits Madrid to meet Sánchez, Felipe VI and Latin American leaders at the Ibero-American Summit, aiming to boost support for Ukraine and closer ties with Latin America.

absaetze.t: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Madrid on Wednesday for a series of high-level meetings coinciding with the Ibero-American Summit. His visit, which was kept secret for security reasons until his plane landed, includes a schedule of meetings with international leaders over the summit's two days.
ADVERTISEMENT

Zelenskyy will take part in a meeting on Thursday with several of the leaders who have travelled to the capital, among them UN Secretary-General António Guterres and European Council President António Costa.

The presence of the Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is also expected, along with other Ibero-American representatives. Besides this meeting, the Ukrainian president will hold bilateral talks with Sánchez and with Spanish King Felipe VI.

Holding the summit in Madrid is also an opportunity for Kyiv to strengthen its contacts with Latin American countries, a region where the war triggered by the Russian invasion continues to generate opposing positions. According to government sources, Zelenskyy plans to hold meetings with representatives of several of the 22 Ibero-American delegations present in the capital.
Zelenskyy to meet country leaders in a heated context
Zelenskyy confirmed his arrival on social media, saying "our top priority is strengthening Ukraine's air defences, protecting our people, and expanding defence cooperation and production."
"Further support steps are being prepared," the Ukrainian president added, without providing details on the measures or the leaders he would meet.
The far-right presidents of Argentina and Chile, Javier Milei and Jose Antonio Kast, as well as Bolivian conservative Rodrigo Paz, are among the Latin American heads of state in the Spanish capital.
Two weeks ago, Milei made a visit to Madrid where he called Sanchez a "disgraceful dictator" and urged Spaniards to "kick out" his Socialists in the election.

The firebrand libertarian has made several unofficial visits to Spain since becoming Argentina's president in 2023, but has never met Sanchez, instead supporting the conservative and far-right opposition as well as launching into long diatribes against socialism.
The Ibero-American format has lost influence in recent years, and reversing that trend is the key goal of the group's 30th summit in Madrid.
At the last summit, held in Ecuador in 2024, a historically low four heads of state turned up and the divided participants failed to adopt a final declaration.
This year, the seven Latin American presidents in attendance will illustrate the region's tilt to the right after a slew of electoral victories for allies of Trump.

Further complicating the scene for Sanchez is the absence of his leftist allies in Latin America's powerhouses: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Brazil's newly re-elected veteran Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
'The best response is an open economy,' Felipe VI

Against a backdrop of economic uncertainty and international tensions, Felipe VI argued for an open economy and a move away from protectionism. "The best response does not lie in protectionism, but in an open economy based on equal rules for everyone," he told Ibero-American business leaders gathered in Madrid.

The Spanish King rejected the idea that the response should be to close off the national economies or raise trade barriers. Instead, he advocated greater openness and cooperation between countries that share values and objectives. In this regard, he highlighted the potential of Ibero-America as a space to deepen ties and generate new economic opportunities.

The region has, he stressed, significant energy resources and strategic raw materials, including critical minerals and rare earths, which could place it in a prominent position in the new international economic landscape. To make the most of these opportunities, Felipe VI stressed the importance of having "stable environments, legal certainty and solid, transparent institutions".

These are conditions he considers essential for attracting investment and building trust. "Trust is one of our most valuable assets and, allow me to say, also one of those we can most easily lose", he said.

Finally, the Monarch stressed the importance of continuing to tighten ties between the European Union and Latin America and the Caribbean, a relationship he sees as essential for tackling today's economic challenges and seizing the opportunities offered by a rapidly changing international landscape.
Albares defends the Ibero-American Summit amid absences

It fell to the Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, to play down the empty seats. "It is absolutely not a forum in decline," he insisted on Wednesday before the foreign ministers' meeting. His argument is that all 22 countries have someone in Madrid, at least their foreign minister, and that those who are not coming either rarely travel or are facing internal problems that prevent them from being away for several days.

Absent, among others, are Lula da Silva, Claudia Sheinbaum and Delcy Rodríguez, and with them several of the presidents closest to Sánchez, who instead finds himself alongside Chilean José Antonio Kast and Milei, at the opposite end of the political spectrum. Albares chose to look back. Only three heads of state attended the Cuenca meeting in 2024, and compared with that, ten seems a success to him.

On the ideological clash, the minister said the community had always been diverse in the political colour of its governments and that its strength lay in putting a common voice above differences he regarded as temporary. The Ibero-American Secretary-General, Andrés Allamand, describes it as "the summit of reaffirmation".

items.titel: Navy unfairly evaluated Saildrone MUSV proposal, court finds
items.anriss: The court found that the Navy “engaged in disparate treatment” toward Saildrone’s MUSV proposal, according to an opinion unsealed Wednesday.

absaetze.t: PARIS — The US Navy unfairly evaluated maritime drone manufacturer Saildrone’s proposal for the service’s medium unmanned surface vessel (MUSV) program, according to a ruling from the US Court of Federal Claims.
As a result, the Navy must reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal within the next two months, and is barred from spending a large chunk of its MUSV budget until that process is complete.

Saildrone and maritime tech startup Blue Water Autonomy filed lawsuits in June challenging the Navy’s decision to eliminate their respective proposals — Saildrone’s Spectre and Blue Water Autonomy’s Liberty — from the MUSV competition. The companies argued that their platforms met the Navy’s requirements for the MUSV marketplace, which launched in March, and that the service didn’t stick to its own evaluation guidance in the request for proposals (RFP).

“The Court finds that the Navy engaged in disparate treatment, and thus, acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner in its review of Saildrone’s proposal,” Judge Philip Hadji wrote in his opinion, which was originally issued Oct. 30 and publicly released on Wednesday.

The Navy originally disqualified Saildrone from advancing to on-water testing due to discrepancies between the company’s proposal and a summary document known as a J-8 Placemat, which is related to the maximum displacement of the design. The opinion said the Navy “eliminated Saildrone because its Placemat reported loaded displacements exceeded the stated maximum displacement.”

However, the court determined that Saildrone received disparate treatment compared to other firms because the Navy advanced a proposal from Sea Machines despite similar issues involving maximum displacement. It’s unclear which Sea Machines vessel — either the Steamracer of the Steamrunner — the Navy evaluated, the opinion said. However, the court noted that the distinction did not affect its finding.

“Because the Navy accepted from Sea Machines a Placemat that either reported both payload-condition displacements above the stated ‘Max Displacement,’ as Saildrone’s did (STEAMRUNNER), or left those fields blank (STEAMRACER), the Court finds the Navy’s subsequent treatment of the proposals disparately favored Sea Machines and arbitrarily held Saildrone to a higher standard,” the opinion said.

Under the ruling, the court ordered the Navy to reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal within 60 days, applying the same evaluation approach it used for companies that advanced in the competition. The ruling also prohibits the Navy from relying on its previously withdrawn findings under two other evaluation criteria to eliminate Saildrone.
The court also barred the Navy from spending more than $1.5 billion of the $2.1 billion allocated for the program on production until it completes that reevaluation.
A US Navy spokesperson told Breaking Defense that it will comply with the court’s order and reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal to determine if it will qualify for on-water testing.

“The future of naval warfare will be fought on the water, not in a courtroom,” Richard Jenkins, Saildrone’s founder and CEO, said in a statement on Monday. “We are eager to move beyond this litigation and return our entire focus to delivering world-leading maritime autonomy for the US Navy, to help secure America’s future maritime dominance. This ruling is a win for fair competition, for taxpayers, and for national security.”
Blue Water Ruling
However, Hadji reached a different conclusion regarding Blue Water Autonomy, determining that “the Navy reasonably rated Blue Water unacceptable.”

The service eliminated the company from the competition for several reasons, including because it claimed that Blue Water’s test vessel — a twin-hulled catamaran — was not “representative” of its production vessel, an axe-bow monohull.
However, Blue Water Autonomy argued that the Navy deviated from its own evaluation requirements because “[h]ull and machinery plants are not listed as assets to be evaluated in the testing.”

The court disagreed, and the opinion said that “the Court concludes that ‘representative’ unambiguously calls for comparing the test vessel with the production vessel,” and noted that the solicitation did not exclude hull form or propulsion architecture from that comparison.

Even so, Austin Gray, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Blue Water Autonomy, said in a statement to Breaking Defense that “nothing about the test vessel was core to our technology, our ship, or our product.”
Gray also said the Navy has made positive changes in Phase II of its MUSV program the service unveiled in September.

For example, Phase I required proposals to travel 2,500 nautical miles at 25 knots in sea state 4 conditions with a payload capacity of two 40-foot containers. In contrast, Phase II requires that proposals include a payload capacity of at least two standard 20-foot shipping containers and eliminates the high-speed requirement.

“The Navy’s new leadership team has already leaned ahead and fixed problems highlighted by the protest,” Gray said. “The Medium USV Phase II program steers away from the prescriptive, compliance-centric testing rules of the previous competition, a change made by thoughtful Navy acquisition professionals months ago.”

Christopher Miller, Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for robotic and autonomous systems (DRPM RAS) recently acknowledged some difficulties that Phase I requirements presented for industry. He said the Navy wants to “open the aperture” for new entrants and increase options for other services that may be interested in the capabilities.

“What I’m trying to do is also give more industry opportunities for companies that have something ready to go,” Miller told reporters in September. “Obviously with Phase I, there were some more challenging requirements that they had to meet, and so I’m trying to back off of those so that I can have a healthy, competitive industrial base and really use that to help us identify near-term opportunities to meet our operational demands.”

items.titel: Amid Iran conflict, ‘non-hostile’ deaths of 2 US airmen raise overseas toll
items.anriss: Two unidentified U.S. airmen died last week in “non-hostile” incidents amid the war in Iran, raising the number of American fatalities since the war began to 23.

absaetze.t: Two unidentified U.S. airmen died last week in “non-hostile” incidents amid the war in Iran, raising the number of American fatalities since the war began to 23.

The two airmen are listed under the “non-hostile” category in the Pentagon’s recently updated Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS, meaning their deaths are not related to direct combat operations. One of the deaths was illness- or injury-related, and the other is listed as “pending,” according to the DCAS.
One airman was an active-duty service member, an Air Force spokesperson told Military Times, while the other was in the Air National Guard.

Although typical Department of Defense policy dictates that the names of deceased service members be released to the public 24 hours after next of kin notifications, the Air Force has yet to announce their identities. The spokesperson declined to comment on why their names have been withheld thus far and if the service has been in contact with their families.
Both airmen were white men and mid- to senior-enlisted personnel in E5 to E9 grades, according to DCAS. One was between 31 and 35, while the other was over 35.
One of the airmen passed away in the U.S. Central Command’s area of responsibility, which spans from Northeast Africa across the Middle East to Central and South Asia, the spokesperson said.
The other airman died in the United States; however, the spokesperson declined to comment on where the second airman was operating out of and how they were transported to the U.S.
CENTCOM referred Military Times to the Air Force when asked for comment.
The airman whose death is listed as “pending” is under investigation currently, the spokesperson said, but did not specify by which department.
Another service member whose death was listed as “pending” in DCAS was an Army captain who suffered a medical incident while aboard a military flight on the way to Saudi Arabia in late September.

DCAS lists both of the airmen’s deaths under the Overseas Operations category, instead of Operation Epic Fury, with a Pentagon official telling Military Times it is because the U.S. deems Epic Fury as concluded. The Overseas Operations lists the start date as July 7, aligned with the continued U.S. pressure campaign against Iran.
Officials have been tight-lipped on the exact date Epic Fury was considered terminated, but a defense official previously specified May 5 to Military Times.

The Pentagon’s classification of the operation as an Overseas Operation category faced criticism from Democratic members of Congress, who accused Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth of trying to hide the casualties.

The Overseas Operation category now includes eight service members: four listed as hostile and four as non-hostile. Combining the two categories together makes for a total of 23 service members who have lost their lives since the war in Iran began on Feb. 28, with the Epic Fury category listing 15.

In total, 866 service members have been wounded in action since the war’s beginning across both categories. That includes 417 under Operation Epic Fury and 449 in Overseas Operations, according to DCAS.

items.titel: Daniel Sikkema Sentenced to Life for Murder of Art Dealer Brent Sikkema
items.anriss: Daniel Sikkema, 56, has been sentenced to life in prison for his role in the murder-for-hire of his estranged husband, New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the …

absaetze.t: The 56-year-old man is accountable for a "cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot," said US Attorney Jamie McDonald.
November 4, 2026 — 2 min read

Daniel Sikkema, 56, has been sentenced to life in prison for his role in the murder-for-hire of his estranged husband, New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) announced today, November 4.

Brent Sikkema, the 75-year-old co-owner of the Manhattan gallery Sikkema Jenkins & Company, was found dead in his Rio de Janeiro residence in January 2024. He was stabbed 18 times. Two months after the incident, Daniel Sikkema was arrested in Manhattan on charges of passport fraud and later received additional counts of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder for hire, and conspiracy to murder a person in a foreign country. A federal jury found him guilty on those charges following a two-week trial in May.

"Today’s life sentence holds Daniel Sikkema accountable for a cold, calculated murder-for-hire plot that resulted in the murder of his husband, Brent Sikkema,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a press release. Daniel Sikkema was also sentenced to five years of supervised release.

“For months, the defendant manipulated friends, family, and employees to execute a killing driven by greed. His actions demonstrated a profound disregard for human life and the rule of law," McDonald continued.

Daniel Sikkema had paid the couple's former security guard, Alejandro Prevez, to kill his husband as their divorce proceedings dragged on. Shortly after the fatal stabbing, Daniel Sikkema sent $5,000 to Prevez and promised future payments. The former security guard was arrested by Brazilian law enforcement four days after the murder and still awaits charges in Brazilian courts, according to the press release.

Brent Sikkema co-founded Sikkema Malloy Jenkins (then called Sikkema Jenkins Gallery) with his business partner, Michael Jenkins, in the early 1990s, where he showed artists including Kara Walker, Sheila Hicks, and Vik Muniz. The gallery currently represents more than 30 artists.

items.titel: Hong Kong artists create a poetic moment in Venice
items.anriss: Hong Kong’s collateral exhibition at the Venice Biennale, now in its 25th year, features the Hong Kong-born artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui

absaetze.t: For Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, the Hong Kong-born artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui are training visitors’ attention on the quiet moments and subtle details connecting both cities. The exhibition, marking the 25th anniversary of Hong Kong’s first participation in the Venice Biennale, is curated by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA) and continues until 22 November. It is housed in a historic Venetian residential building in the floating city’s Campo della Tana neighbourhood, a setting that underlines the meditative, lived-in quality to the works.

“What we hope visitors take away from the exhibition is a moment of reflection,” says Dr Maria Mok, the director of the HKMoA. “Through Kingsley and Angel’s attention to everyday details, we hope visitors feel invited to slow down and become more attentive to their surroundings, even within the hustle and intensity of urban life.”

One of Kingsley Ng’s installations, for instance, Laundry Nocturne (2026), consists of a projection and soundscape that evoke the play of light across laundry hung between buildings. It was inspired by the artist’s experience visiting Venice, where billowing laundry on clotheslines is still common, though for Ng it also evoked memories of Hong Kong.

“The laundry becomes a point of entry into a wider soundscape of nighttime labour: recordings from a wastewater treatment plant, a newspaper-printing facility and a postal sorting centre evoke the work that continues while much of the city sleeps,” Ng says. “These modest, often overlooked processes that keep a city alive do not only connect Venice and Hong Kong. They are like a low hum in almost every city, to be picked up by an ear that doesn’t only listen to loud grandeur.”

For her installations, Angel Hui shines a spotlight on humble features of Hong Kong’s everyday life, including goldfish in plastic bags and a neighbour’s ornate but faded window frame. In her magical rendering, glowing plastic bags embroidered with goldfish motifs are suspended overhead, while a handwrought iron window made by Hui and traditional metalsmiths rotates slowly in the gallery.

“In Hong Kong, a goldfish bag is an everyday object; in Venice, it seemed almost precious—delicate and exposed,” Hui says. “The experience reminded me that a work does not need to be grand to hold meaning. Sometimes, its poetry lies in inviting us to look more attentively, and to meet the familiar with tenderness.”

Both artists, through their site-specific installations, encourage visitors to mark a pause while heightening their attention to details of light, sound, colour and texture. This invitation to contemplation is echoed in the exhibition’s title, Fermata, which is a type of musical symbol instructing a performer to hold a note or a pause for an extra moment, and the term for the places where Venetian vaporettos stop to let off and pick up passengers. For Hui, this title and its dual meanings resonate across the exhibition’s disparate locales.

“The difference in pace is pronounced: Hong Kong often presses forward, while Venice seems to make room for pause,” she says. “This is why Fermata—a moment of stopping, of stillness—felt so resonant. In both cities, the ordinary endures, and in that endurance, everyday objects acquire a quiet radiance.”
The exhibition’s title and installations also complement the theme of this year’s Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys, set by the late curator Koyo Kouoh.

“I come to see the works as experiences to return to and live alongside,” Ng says. “For me, that is one meaning of In Minor Keys: making time for the ordinary and immediate—the air, light and weather around us—and becoming more attentive to our presence within them.”

The artists’ ability to turn familiar objects and moments into tableaux where time pauses and senses are heightened is key to the exhibition’s power. It allows their installations to resonate across localities, from the Venetian Lagoon to Hong Kong’s cityscape.

“The artworks merge into the Venetian neighbourhood, from laundry hanging across nearby alleys and above our courtyard exhibition space to the view of the neighbourhood outside Kingsley’s Laundry Nocturne gallery, to wrought-iron windows that echo Angel’s work,” Dr Mok says. “All these details are blurring the boundary between the exhibition and its surroundings. They also show how small moments of daily life can quietly synchronise across different cities and audiences.”
Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, Campo della Tana, Castello 2126, 30122, Venice, until 22 November 2026

items.titel: As it expands, Provincetown’s Fine Arts Work Center prioritises access and affordability
items.anriss: The Cape Cod community’s local arts centre is planning for future growth, bolstered by $1.2m in support from the municipal board

absaetze.t: Provincetown, the harbour community perched on the tip of the Cape Cod peninsula in Massachusetts, has a well-earned reputation as a haven for artists, but that status is under threat due to a lack of affordable housing. Geographically secluded and aesthetically distinctive, the town, which experienced an influx of Portuguese sailors in the 1850s, has attracted artists for almost a century, particularly queer painters, writers and poets.

Provincetown’s Fine Arts Work Center(FAWC) has been at the heart of this creative community since it was founded in 1968 by a group that included the painters Robert Motherwell, Myron Stout, Jack Tworkov and Fritz Bultman. The painter Sam Messer and Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Mary Oliver were among the centre’s early residents, followed in ensuing decades by artists including Lisa Yuskavage, Jack Pierson, Ellen Gallagher, Jeffrey Gibson, Firelei Báez, Elliot Hundley, Jacolby Satterwhite and Jennifer Packer.

Today, the non-profit grants artists access and community in a town that is among the most expensive in New England during the summer season. Providing room and support for queer artists remains a priority. The Venezuelan artist Miguel Braceli, for instance, completed his 2024 residency by orchestrating the public performance True Love’s Kiss, in which strangers were invited to lock lips at the granite breakwater on the shore’s very western tip.

Located in the Provincetown’s residential east end, the FAWC is best known for its residency programme, which provides ten artist fellows and ten writers with lodging and studio space for seven months every year, between October and April. Among this year’s artist residents are Abigail Dudley, Alina Perez, Nasim Hantehzadeh and L.J. Roberts.

“People have come here for generations to live their identities to the fullest and they have heavily contributed to the artistic creativity that makes Provincetown what is,” Sharon Polli , the centre’s executive director, tells The Art Newspaper. “The unique experience residents feel the second they drive down Route 6 or step off the ferry comes out in the work created here.”

The centre has been in a continuous state of expansion and renovation for much of its 58-year history. What was once the longtime Provincetown resident Hans Hoffman’s studio is now a fraction of the centre’s main grounds, named Days Lumberyard, which includes multiple living units, studios, offices, an auditorium, a gallery space, an outdoor area and a printshop that still houses Motherwell’s own press. The centre acquired a heating supply building in 1972 for around $120,000 and has gradually transformed its coal bins and other disused or dilapidated areas into its main hub.

Polli says the lumberyard’s growth and importance to the community are proof of “Provincetown being a place where there has always been room for artists and writers who maintain the town’s cultural identity” since the middle of the 20th century. The centre operates on an annual budget of around $3m, $600,000 of which this year was raised at its annual summer gala at the Pilgrim Monument at the Provincetown Museum.

The centre’s core role in maintaining the town’s artistic and intellectual identity has recently been officially acknowledged. The municipal board made a pledge this past summer to grant the centre $1.5m toward a planned $12m transformation of its 4 Brewster Street building. Located around the corner from the main FAWC complex, the lot the centre acquired in 1997 is in line for a totally new build. The Boston-based firm Hacin Architects was selected to double the housing square footage for fellows and staff, while adding a community space and a rooftop garden.

“We are hoping that the municipal support will help us leverage private funding,” Polli says. She and her team of 12 full-time employees keep the conversation and cultural exchange active throughout the off-seasons by offering a community-oriented programming. The year-round calendar includes FAWC Fridays, group exhibitions with past fellows, Queer Week, workshops and public talks with artists such as Catherine Opie, Ilana Savdie and Doron Langberg.

Polli says the centre’s off-season programming is even “more important than anything we do rest of the year because we give people a place to engage with high-calibre dialogues where many locals have working practices”.

items.titel: So You’ve Been Invited to Documenta 16. Here’s Our Advice.
items.anriss: Over the past few months, several artist friends who have been invited to participate in the upcoming documenta 16 have contacted us for advice, asking whether they should accept, refuse early on, or accept for now and withdraw at a later …

absaetze.t: As two documenta 15 artists who were mercilessly vilified due to our support of Palestine, here’s what you need to consider when you make your choice.
November 4, 2026 — 7 min read

Over the past few months, several artist friends who have been invited to participate in the upcoming documenta 16 have contacted us for advice, asking whether they should accept, refuse early on, or accept for now and withdraw at a later stage. As two artists who participated in documenta 15, we understand the dilemma. An invitation to documenta is not something one receives thoughtlessly. It is hard to turn down, and these days, it is also becoming hard to accept.

A few years ago, exhibiting at documenta was considered a lifetime achievement. But after the multi-faceted attacks on Palestinian artists and works of pro-Palestinian art at documenta 15 — and the collapse of the German state’s moral standing through its support for the genocide in Palestine and considering Israel its Staatsräson (“reason of state”) — this assumption has been shattered. There is no meaningful distance between the German state and its art institutions: Almost every museum, Kunsthalle, and festival, documenta included, is funded by the federal, regional, or municipal government, and thus steered by the conditions those funders set. As such, artists have to seriously ask themselves whether participating in documenta 16 will negatively affect one's career and well-being.

Our friends ask us for advice because of what the two of us, among many others, went through during documenta 15. We were subjected to severe and vicious attacks by the German media, political activists, politicians, and the establishment, built on unfounded, fabricated, and destructive accusations of antisemitism, which eventually led to attacks and vandalism of our exhibition venues, alongside those of other artists. This experience left scars on our lives and careers, making it hard to apply for jobs, funding, or exhibition opportunities. The stress and burnout we had to endure as a result of these attacks were enormous, and the energy it took came from our work and our lives — that toll can’t be overstated. This is why we decided to stay anonymous in this piece: to avoid any return to the stress and fear we had to deal with, which still haunts us even after nearly five years.

To those friends who are asking, and others who are wondering, we will not tell you whether to participate in documenta 16 or not. This is your own decision about what you wish to lend your voice to — personally, politically, creatively. But we can tell you what we wish we had known, and what you need to consider when you make your choice.

Since the beginning of the current genocide in Palestine, the German cultural scene has been in crisis. It has lost its credibility and shown how much it functions as the soft hand of state power. It has no independence from state politics and is unable to stand up against the position of the state due to the way arts and culture are funded in Germany. In 2019, the Bundestag passed a non-binding resolution calling for federal funding to be withheld from any organization or project that supports Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS). Non-binding as it was, it became a political tool to suppress any institutional support for the Palestinian cause. Another resolution in November 2024 tied public funding to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s controversial definition of antisemitism — which documenta officially adopted in early 2025. The rest of Germany’s major cultural institutions, except for a few independent ones, bent with little resistance. Like the others, documenta depends on state and federal funding; and like the others, it has no spine. German institutions are struggling to emerge from this crisis and regain their credibility without revising their positions or standing up to political pressure. At this point and under these conditions, documenta as an institution will likely benefit more from your participation than you will.
